sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s. The same change gives तुष्टिस्त्वं.
Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra.
Visarga after i, before a vowel, appears as r.

morph.note: Possessive taddhita -इन् (‘having’) on खड्ग gives खड्गिन् ‘sword-bearer’; the feminine adds -ई. The verse builds five such forms in a row (खड्गिनी, शूलिनी, गदिनी, चक्रिणी, and in 1.81 शङ्खिनी, चापिनी).
The n of the suffix turns retroflex (ṇ) because r stands earlier in the same word with nothing to block it; compare गदिनी and शूलिनी, where there is no r.
Action noun in -ति (ktin) from √क्षम् ‘to endure’; the nasal of the root appears as न् before त. शान्तिः from √शम् is formed the same way.

mantras.anvaya: त्वं लज्जा पुष्टिः तथा तुष्टिः, त्वं शान्तिः क्षान्तिः एव च (असि)। (त्वं) खड्गिनी शूलिनी घोरा गदिनी तथा चक्रिणी (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A list of predicate nominatives with त्वम् and an understood असि, continuing the list of 1.77–79: first five virtues, then a run of feminine possessive adjectives naming her weapons.
mantras.lit: (You are) modesty, nourishment and likewise contentment; you (are) peace and forbearance too. (You are) sword-bearing, trident-bearing, terrible, mace-bearing and likewise discus-bearing;
mantras.tr: You are modesty, nourishment and contentment; you are peace, and patience too. You bear the sword and the trident; you are terrible; you carry the mace and the discus;

comm.t: Brahmā’s list turns in mid-verse from inner qualities to weapons. Modesty, nourishment, contentment, peace and forbearance are the gentlest powers of a person; the next line arms the same Goddess and calls her घोरा, ‘terrible’. The hymn makes no division between the two.

Several of these qualities return in the yā devī hymn of chapter 5 as forms in which the Devī abides in all beings: क्षान्ति (5.38-40), लज्जा (5.44-46), शान्ति (5.47-49) and तुष्टि (5.68-70). The weapons named in 1.80–81 match the dhyāna of Mahākālī that the Gita Press pāṭha sets before the first carita (sword, discus, mace, arrows, bow, iron club, trident, bhuśuṇḍī, a head, conch); the hymn names all of them except the head. The dhyāna is liturgical tradition, not part of the Purāṇa.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same names as single epithets: 443 तुष्टिः, 444 पुष्टिः, 447 शान्तिः and 740 लज्जा. The overlap is in vocabulary for the Goddess’s powers; the two texts are separate works.

samasa.vigraha: बाणाः च भुशुण्डी च परिघः च बाणभुशुण्डीपरिघाः; ते आयुधानि यस्याः सा
samasa.literal: she whose weapons are arrows, bhuśuṇḍī and iron club
samasa.sense: armed with arrows, the bhuśuṇḍī and the iron club; भुशुण्डी is a missile weapon whose exact form is not certain

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (अशेष itself a nañ-bahuvrīhi: न विद्यते शेषः यस्य तत्)
samasa.sense: than every gentle thing there is

samasa.type: prādi tatpuruṣa (the prefix अति ‘beyond, exceedingly’ as first member)

morph.note: Comparative in -तर (taddhita) on सौम्य, feminine -तरा. The thing surpassed stands in the ablative: सौम्यतरा अशेषसौम्येभ्यः ‘gentler than all gentle things’.
Taddhita from सोम ‘the moon (Soma)’ with vṛddhi of the first syllable: ‘of the moon’s nature’, hence cool, mild, benign — the opposite of घोरा in 1.80.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) शङ्खिनी चापिनी बाणभुशुण्डीपरिघायुधा (असि)। सौम्या, अशेषसौम्येभ्यः सौम्यतरा, अतिसुन्दरी तु (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The weapon-list of 1.80 ends; the second line sets a gentle triad against it. The ablative अशेषसौम्येभ्यः is taken with the comparative सौम्यतरा, which requires one. It can also be read with अतिसुन्दरी (‘more beautiful than all gentle things’); the comparative is the stronger claim on it.
mantras.lit: conch-bearing, bow-bearing, having arrows, bhuśuṇḍī and iron club as weapons; gentle, more gentle than all gentle things, and exceedingly beautiful.
mantras.tr: you bear the conch and the bow, and your weapons are arrows, the bhuśuṇḍī and the iron club. Yet you are gentle — gentler than every gentle thing — and beautiful beyond measure.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Yet’ renders the contrast the verse makes by placing सौम्या straight after the weapons; the Sanskrit has only तु ‘and, moreover’.

comm.t: The arming of the Goddess is completed — conch, bow, arrows, bhuśuṇḍī and iron club — and in the same breath she is called gentle, gentler than all gentle things, surpassingly beautiful. The terrible one of 1.80 (घोरा) and the gentle one here (सौम्या) are one.

The pairing of the fierce (घोर) and the gentle (सौम्य) is basic to the Śākta picture of the Goddess: the same Devī is worshipped in terrible and benign forms. This hymn states the pairing outright before the stories of chapters 2–13 show it in action.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has सौम्या as name 910. The adjective is common; the shared word shows a shared idiom of praise, not a borrowing.
A modern reflection: the hymn does not ask the reader to choose between a gentle and a fierce divinity. Protection and tenderness are offered as aspects of one care.

samasa.vigraha: पराणि च अपराणि च परापराणि, तेषाम्
samasa.literal: of the higher and the lower
samasa.sense: of all things, high and low; the Goddess is the highest even among the highest
samasa.alt: पर and अपर can also be taken as the transcendent and the immanent (the supreme and the manifest), so ‘supreme over both the transcendent and the manifest’. The compound is the same dvandva either way.

samasa.sense: the supreme Īśvarī, the Goddess as ruler of all; internal sandhi a + ī → e (आद्गुणः, 6.1.87), the feminine first member taking its masculine form

samasa.type: samāhāra dvandva (neuter singular), here used as an adjective of वस्तु
samasa.sense: whatever is, or is not; with वा the two are alternatives: ‘existent or non-existent’

samasa.vigraha: अखिलम् आत्मा यस्याः सा अखिलात्मिका, तत्सम्बुद्धौ
samasa.literal: O you whose self is the whole
samasa.sense: O you who are the self of everything — the same formation as स्वरात्मिका (1.73) and मात्रात्मिका (1.74)

morph.note: The interrogative किम् with the particle चित् becomes an indefinite: ‘anything’. With the relative यत् it generalises: यत् किंचित् ‘whatever at all’. क्वचित् (क्व ‘where?’ + चित्) is the adverb ‘anywhere’.
Vocative singular of an ā-stem feminine: the final ā becomes e (अखिलात्मिका → अखिलात्मिके), as in देवि from देवी with shortening.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अखिलात्मिके, त्वम् एव परापराणां परमा परमेश्वरी (असि)। यत् च किंचित् सत् असत् वा वस्तु क्वचित् (अस्ति) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete statement. The second opens a relative clause (यत् … वस्तु) whose correlative तस्य सर्वस्य comes in 1.83.
mantras.lit: Of the higher and the lower the highest, you alone are the supreme Īśvarī. And whatever thing (there is) anywhere, existent or non-existent, O Self of all —
mantras.tr: Highest of all things high and low, you alone are the supreme Sovereign. And whatever thing there is, anywhere, whether it is or is not, O Soul of all —
mantras.tr_note: The second line is completed by 1.83 (‘of all that, you are the power’).

comm.t: Brahmā moves from listing names to a claim about everything: she is the highest over high and low alike, and the second line begins to say that whatever exists, or does not exist, belongs to her. The sentence finishes in 1.83.
सत् and असत् are often explained in Indian thought as the manifest (the effect) and the unmanifest (the cause). Read so, the verse leaves nothing, manifest or latent, outside the Goddess.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 790 परापरा, 396 परमेश्वरी and 661 सदसद्रूपधारिणी (‘bearing the forms of being and non-being’). The concepts are the same; the formulations belong to each text.

sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant is written as anusvāra, twice.
i before a becomes y (पाति + अत्ति → पात्यत्ति). The t of जगत् stays unvoiced before p (खरि च, 8.4.55); the words are only written together.

samasa.alt: It can also be read as two words, जगत् (acc.) + स्रष्टा, with the agent noun taking an object like a verb, which keeps the line’s three जगत् parallel (creates / protects / devours the world). The sense is the same; the printed text joins all three, so print decides nothing.

morph.note: Passive present of √स्तु: the root vowel lengthens before the passive marker -य- (स्तू-य-), with the ātmanepada second-person ending -से. ‘Are you praised?’ — here rhetorical: ‘how can you be praised?’
√अद् (adādi) adds the ending directly to the root: अद् + ति → अत्ति, with d unvoiced before t.
स्रष्टृ ‘creator’ is the agent noun (tṛc) of √सृज्; nom. sg. स्रष्टा. The root’s vowel and r change places (सृज् → स्रष्) before the suffix.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य सर्वस्य या शक्तिः, सा त्वम् (असि)। तदा (त्वं) किं स्तूयसे? यया त्वया, यः जगत्स्रष्टा (यः) जगत् पाति (यः) जगत् अत्ति, (सः अपि निद्रावशं नीतः) —
mantras.anvaya_en: Line one completes 1.82 with the correlative pair या … सा. Line two opens a long relative clause: यया त्वया is the agent of नीतः in 1.84, and यः … जगत् describes the one who was put to sleep.
mantras.lit: Of all that, the power which (it has) — that (power) you (are). How then are you to be praised? By whom — by you — he who (is) the creator of the world, (who) protects the world, (who) devours the world,
mantras.tr: of all that, you are the power. How then can anyone praise you? You, by whom he who creates the world, sustains the world and devours the world
mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues into 1.84: ‘— even he has been brought under the sway of sleep’.

comm.t: The argument of the hymn is made plain: if she is the power (शक्ति) of everything that is, then every act — praise included — is already hers, and no praise can reach her. The second line names the one she has overcome: the god who creates, preserves and consumes the world, i.e. the sleeping Viṣṇu.

In Śākta thought śakti is the power by which any being acts, inseparable from it. The verse applies the idea to the gods themselves: even the agent of creation, preservation and destruction acts through her, and when she withdraws (as sleep) he does not act at all.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) gives the three acts to the Goddess directly: 264 सृष्टिकर्त्री (creator), 266 गोप्त्री (protector), 268 संहारिणी (destroyer). The Devī Māhātmya keeps them with a god and makes her the power behind him.
A modern reflection: the hymn admits its own limit. To say ‘how can you be praised?’ in the middle of praise is a way of keeping words honest about what they cannot hold.

sandhi.note: -aḥ before a becomes -o, and the following a is elided (avagraha).
a + ī → e (इह + ईश्वरः → इहेश्वरः); the m of स्तोतुम् joins the following vowel unchanged.
-aḥ before a vowel other than a: the visarga becomes y, which is dropped, leaving the vowels apart.

samasa.sense: the sway of sleep; वशं नी ‘bring under control’ is an idiom

morph.note: Past passive participle of √नी used as a finite verb (‘has been led’). With नी the destination stays in the accusative in the passive (निद्रावशम्), while the person led becomes the subject (सः).
Infinitive of purpose with ईश्वरः ‘able’: कः … स्तोतुम् ईश्वरः ‘who is able to praise?’
Literally ‘master, lord’; with an infinitive it means ‘having power to’. The word picks up परमेश्वरी of 1.82: she is the Īśvarī, and no one is ईश्वर to praise her.

mantras.anvaya: सः अपि निद्रावशं नीतः। इह त्वां स्तोतुं कः ईश्वरः? विष्णुः, अहम्, ईशानः एव च शरीरग्रहणं (त्वया कारिताः) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the relative clause of 1.83 (यया त्वया … सः अपि … नीतः) and asks a rhetorical question. The second line names three subjects whose verb, कारिताः, comes in 1.85.
mantras.lit: — even he has been led into the control of sleep. Who here is able to praise you? Viṣṇu, I and Īśāna too, (have been made by you to undertake) the taking of bodies —
mantras.tr: — even he has been brought under the sway of sleep. Who here has the power to praise you? Viṣṇu, I myself and Īśāna
mantras.tr_note: The second line continues into 1.85: ‘have been made by you to take on bodies’.

comm.t: The creator, preserver and consumer of the world lies asleep by her power, so no one is fit to praise her. Brahmā then names the three gods — Viṣṇu, himself and Īśāna (Śiva) — and in the next verse says that their very bodies are her doing.

Śākta readers take 1.84–85 as a foundation for the Goddess’s priority over the three gods: the three who create, preserve and dissolve are themselves made to take form by her. The speaker is Brahmā, one of the three, which gives the admission its weight.
A modern reflection: the most capable figures in the story are shown to depend on a power they did not make. The hymn turns the gods’ own testimony into a lesson in humility.
